power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Cannabis use is common and increases appetite, which may lead to large eating episodes that overlap with binge eating pathology.
However, whether large eating episodes are related to health outcomes among individuals who use cannabis is not known.

To address this gap, we analyzed seven cycles of the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES; 2005 to 2018) including 18,709 adults aged 20 to 59 years (2,578 current, 7,394 past, and 8,737 never cannabis users).
A large eating episode was defined as an eating occasion of at least 1,500 kcal on either of two 24-hour dietary recalls.
Among current cannabis users, survey-weighted logistic regression with Benjamini-Hochberg correction estimated adjusted associations between large eating episodes and 29 health outcomes.
The weighted prevalence of a large eating episode was 30.3% among current cannabis users, 22.2% among past users, and 19.3% among never users.
Among current users, a large eating episode was associated with higher odds of fair or poor self-rated health (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.75, 95% CI [1.27, 2.41], p < .001, q = .022).
text.formatted: Among current users, a large eating episode was associated with higher odds of fair or poor self-rated health (adjusted odds ratio [OR] = 1.75, 95% CI [1.27, 2.41], p < .001, q = .022).

text.text: No other association remained significant after correction, although nominal associations were observed for household food insecurity, obesity, abdominal obesity, and elevated glycated hemoglobin.
Notably, adults with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode had higher odds of fair or poor health than each of the other three groups (ORs = 1.79 to 1.85, all p < .001).
text.formatted: Notably, adults with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode had higher odds of fair or poor health than each of the other three groups (ORs = 1.79 to 1.85, all p < .001).

text.text: In exploratory analyses, the hazard of death was higher for adults with both exposures after adjustment for age and sex (hazard ratio [HR] = 2.08, 95% CI [1.31, 3.31]), though it did not remain significantly higher after full adjustment (HR = 1.40, 95% CI [0.88, 2.21]).
Findings suggest that asking about eating patterns may help clinicians identify individuals who use cannabis and may be experiencing health-related distress.
Longitudinal studies measuring loss of control over eating, cannabis frequency, and product type are critical for determining whether eating patterns affect health.
Cannabis use has risen sharply in the United States.

Between 2008 and 2022, the per capita rate of past-year use increased by 120% (Caulkins, 2024), and in 2022, daily or near-daily cannabis users outnumbered daily or near-daily drinkers for the first time (Caulkins, 2024).

text.text: Importantly, cannabis is also known to stimulate appetite.
In a controlled study of 82 adults, vaporized cannabis increased the amount of food eaten in the first 30 minutes of access across fat, carbohydrate, and protein (Hume et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In a controlled study of 82 adults, vaporized cannabis increased the amount of food eaten in the first 30 minutes of access across fat, carbohydrate, and protein <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hume et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The same study showed in rats that this effect depended on cannabinoid receptors in the brain and was linked to a higher reward value of food (Hume et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The same study showed in rats that this effect depended on cannabinoid receptors in the brain and was linked to a higher reward value of food <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hume et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Further, another human laboratory study found that cannabis blunted the rise in insulin after a meal and lowered levels of glucagon-like peptide-1 (Farokhnia et al., 2020), which may upregulate appetite.

text.text: However, population studies show a more complicated picture.

Consistent with the above, in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2005 to 2016, adults who currently used cannabis had lower diet quality than past or never users (Gelfand & Tangney, 2021).
text.formatted: Consistent with the above, in the National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) from 2005 to 2016, adults who currently used cannabis had lower diet quality than past or never users <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gelfand & Tangney, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Specifically, the Healthy Eating Index was 51.8 in never users compared with 56.2 in past users and 57.7 in current users.
Unexpectedly, however, body weight did not follow the pattern that appetite effects would predict.

In a 30-year cohort, daily cannabis users had a lower mean body mass index than adults without current use (26.6 compared with 27.7 kg/m², p < .001), and cumulative use and stopping use were not associated with body mass index; the authors attributed the current-use difference to residual confounding (Jakob et al., 2024).

text.text: Similarly, a meta-analysis of randomized trials found a small reduction in body weight with cannabis products (Reis et al., 2024), though the mean difference was only -1.87 kg (95% CI [-3.71, -0.03]), equating to roughly 4 pounds.

text.text: Another meta-analysis of observational studies found lower odds of type 2 diabetes among individuals exposed to cannabis (Mousavi et al., 2023), where the odds ratio was 0.48 (95% CI [0.39, 0.59]).

text.text: In summarizing this literature, a recent review concluded that most studies find no link between cannabis use and weight gain (Goodpaster, 2025).

text.text: As such, appetite stimulation by cannabis does not appear to translate into higher average weight or poorer metabolic health.
However, how specific eating patterns relate to health among individuals who use cannabis has received relatively little study.
This gap is important because average intake can obscure meaningful differences in how individuals eat.
One such difference is the presence of binge eating episodes, which involve eating a large amount of food accompanied by a sense of loss of control over one's eating.
Binge eating is the defining feature of binge eating disorder and is also a diagnostic criterion of bulimia nervosa, which additionally requires recurrent compensatory behaviors (e.g., purging).
In a national interview study of US adults, the lifetime prevalences of binge eating disorder and bulimia nervosa were 2.8% and 1.0%, respectively (Hudson et al., 2007).

text.text: Binge eating is also linked to physical health: in a national sample of 36,309 US adults, it was associated with chronic physical conditions as well as psychiatric disorders (Udo & Grilo, 2019).

text.text: Additionally, reviews describe binge eating disorder as common among adults with type 2 diabetes and suggest that it may worsen glycemic control (Abbott et al., 2018; Harris et al., 2021).

text.text: Cannabis use and binge eating are linked.
Among 165 adults seeking treatment for binge eating, more than 23% had used cannabis in the past three months (Wilkinson et al., 2024).

text.text: Further, a recent review concluded that cannabis use alone is not consistently related to binge eating, whereas cannabis use disorder is associated with loss of control over eating (Goodpaster, 2025).

text.text: These behavioral links have a plausible biological basis, wherein cannabis acts on cannabinoid type 1 (CB1) receptors that are widely expressed in brain regions involved in reward and motivation.
Activation of these receptors raises the reward value of food and the motivation to eat (Bourdy & Befort, 2023).
text.formatted: Activation of these receptors raises the reward value of food and the motivation to eat <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Bourdy & Befort, 2023)</ref>.

text.text: The appetite effects seen in laboratory studies depend on CB1 receptors in the brain (Hume et al., 2026).
text.formatted: The appetite effects seen in laboratory studies depend on CB1 receptors in the brain <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hume et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, individuals who are prone to losing control over eating may be more likely to overeat when cannabis heightens food reward.
Most research on cannabis and eating has focused on binge eating, which requires a subjective sense of loss of control.

However, large national health surveys such as NHANES do not assess loss of control; they do record what individuals eat, allowing for identification of objectively large eating episodes from dietary recalls.
Every binge eating episode contains a large amount of food by definition (American Psychiatric Association, 2013).
text.formatted: Every binge eating episode contains a large amount of food by definition <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Thus, a large eating episode is a necessary component of binge eating that can be measured objectively.
Studying large eating episodes has three advantages.
First, it allows investigators to examine adults in the general population instead of only individuals who seek treatment for loss-of-control eating.
Second, it avoids reliance on an individual's own judgment about whether an episode was out of control.
Third, large eating episodes without loss of control may themselves carry risk.
For example, among adolescents and young adults, overeating without loss of control predicted the later onset of cannabis and other drug use (Sonneville et al., 2013).
text.formatted: For example, among adolescents and young adults, overeating without loss of control predicted the later onset of cannabis and other drug use <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Sonneville et al., 2013)</ref>.

text.text: However, loss of control, more than episode size, is considered the core feature of binge eating (Goldschmidt & Accurso, 2016; Sonneville et al., 2013), and a large eating episode without assessment of loss of control should be considered a broader and less specific marker than binge eating.

text.text: As such, associations observed for large eating episodes would reflect the combined contribution of binge eating and overeating without loss of control, and should not be attributed to diagnostic binge eating alone.
Large eating episodes may relate to health through several pathways.

The first pathway runs through appetite and diet; specifically, cannabis use is linked to greater food reward and motivation to eat (Bourdy & Befort, 2023; Hume et al., 2026), which may then drive larger eating episodes.

text.text: Given that individuals who use cannabis report lower diet quality (Gelfand & Tangney, 2021), these larger eating episodes may then translate into poorer cardiometabolic health (Harris et al., 2021; Udo & Grilo, 2019).

text.text: The second pathway runs through loss of control and psychological distress.
Cannabis use has been linked to weaker inhibitory control during intoxication (Morie & Potenza, 2021), which may then lead to loss of control over eating and elevated caloric intake.

text.text: Binge eating, in turn, predicts elevated psychological distress and eating disorder psychopathology (Goldschmidt & Accurso, 2016; Hudson et al., 2007), which may drive poorer overall health outcomes.

text.text: A third pathway runs through food insecurity.

Cannabis use has been linked to elevated incidence of food insecurity; for example, among young adults, past-month cannabis use predicted 62% higher odds of reporting food insecurity at the next survey wave (Chakraborty et al., 2025).

text.text: Importantly, the reverse direction is also plausible, as food insecurity was associated with cannabis use and cannabis-related spending in the same study (Chakraborty et al., 2025).

text.text: Further, food insecurity has been linked to large eating episodes through an externally enforced "binge-restrict" cycle (Abene et al., 2023; Hazzard et al., 2020).

text.text: Finally, elevated food insecurity is a well-known correlate of poorer physical and mental health, including elevated risk for chronic disease, depression, and anxiety (Arenas et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Finally, elevated food insecurity is a well-known correlate of poorer physical and mental health, including elevated risk for chronic disease, depression, and anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Arenas et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Co-occurring use of other substances may also explain these relationships.
For example, individuals with binge eating who also used cannabis drank more alcohol (Wilkinson et al., 2024).

text.text: Additionally, in another recent multi-state survey, nearly half of adults who smoked cigarettes also used cannabis (Xue et al., 2026).

text.text: Overeating with or without loss of control predicts the later onset of cannabis and other drug use (Sonneville et al., 2013), and substance use itself is highly linked to poorer health and higher mortality.

text.text: For example, current cigarette smoking is associated with more than twice the all-cause mortality rate of never smoking (Thomson et al., 2022).

text.text: Another explanation could produce the same associations without any of these pathways: shared social and economic disadvantage could raise the likelihood of both exposures and of poorer health.
Given that these pathways span physical, psychological, and social domains, outcomes that integrate several domains are especially informative.

Self-rated health is one such outcome, as it is a single question that reflects overall physical and mental well-being and predicts mortality in most community studies of older adults (Dramé et al., 2023).

text.text: As such, self-rated health may register the combined effect of these pathways before disease can be detected by single clinical tests.
Two features suggest that the combination of cannabis use and large eating episodes may be worse than either exposure alone.

First, the pathways described above converge, wherein cannabis may increase the size and frequency of large eating episodes by raising food reward (Hume et al., 2026) and weakening inhibitory control (Morie & Potenza, 2021).

text.text: Accordingly, adults who have both exposures may have episodes that are larger, more frequent, and more distressing than the episodes of adults who do not use cannabis.

Second, adults who have both exposures carry the added risks of each, including lower diet quality (Gelfand & Tangney, 2021), co-occurring alcohol and cigarette use (Wilkinson et al., 2024; Xue et al., 2026), and food insecurity (Abene et al., 2023; Chakraborty et al., 2025).

text.text: Thus, the two exposures may act jointly to compound risk.
To our knowledge, no study to date has examined whether large eating episodes are related to health outcomes among adults who use cannabis.
Thus, the current study used nationally representative data from NHANES to address four aims.
First, we estimated how common large eating episodes were by cannabis-use status.
Second, we tested whether the presence of large eating episodes was associated with any of 29 health outcomes among current cannabis users.
Third, we examined whether poorer health was concentrated among adults who had both current cannabis use and at least one large eating episode.
Fourth, in an exploratory analysis, we examined relationships between cannabis use, large eating episodes, and mortality.
We hypothesized that large eating episodes would be associated with poorer health among current cannabis users and that poorer health would be most evident among adults who had both exposures.

The analyses used R 4.5.1 (R Core Team, 2025) with the survey 4.5 (Lumley, 2024) and survival 3.8-3 (Therneau, 2024) packages.

Two-day dietary weights were divided by the number of cycles contributing to each outcome, or by seven when all cycles contributed.

Secondary and sensitivity analyses.
We repeated the primary logistic regression models using the number of recall days with a large eating episode, first as a count from zero to two and then as separate categories.
To examine whether the associations differed between never, past and current cannabis users, interaction models included large eating episode status, cannabis-use recency and their interaction term.
A separate analysis classified participants into four groups based on current cannabis use and large eating episode status.
These groups comprised neither current cannabis use nor a large eating episode, a large eating episode only, current cannabis use only, and both current cannabis use and a large eating episode.
We compared participants in the group with both with each of the other three groups.

The sensitivity analyses used calorie cutoffs of 1,000 and 2,000 kcal, assessed episodes using only the first recall, required episodes on both recall days, added average daily energy intake, or removed cigarette smoking and alcohol from the models.
All other adjustment variables remained unchanged.
We corrected for multiple testing separately within each set of related analyses across the 29 health outcomes.

In the categorical model, one eating episode day was associated with fair or poor health (OR = 1.86, 95% CI [1.33, 2.59], q = .010), whereas two eating episode days were not (OR = 1.36, 95% CI [0.79, 2.33], q = .548).
The fasting-outcome estimates changed little after additional adjustment for dietary nonresponse.
All three adjusted confidence intervals included 1 (Supplementary Results and Table S1).

The group with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode is compared with each reference group.
The mortality sample included 17,201 participants, of whom 522 died during follow- up (3.0%).

After adjustment for age, age squared and sex, participants with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode had 2.08 times the hazard of death compared with participants with neither current cannabis use nor a large eating episode (HR = 2.08, 95% CI [1.31, 3.31]).
The estimate decreased after full adjustment and was no longer statistically significant (HR = 1.40, 95% CI [0.88, 2.21]).

In the fully adjusted model, the mortality hazard for participants with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode did not clearly differ from current cannabis users without a large eating episode (HR = 1.36, 95% CI [0.74, 2.50]).
It was higher than the estimate for participants who were not current cannabis users but reported a large eating episode (HR = 1.96, 95% CI [1.08, 3.55]).
This exploratory contrast was not corrected for multiple testing.
Fully adjusted analyses restricted to current users were not reported because there were too few deaths for the number of fitted coefficients.

Restricting follow-up to the period beyond month 24 among participants still observed at that point produced no clear difference between participants with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode and those with neither (HR = 1.21, 95% CI [0.64, 2.27]).
Removing cigarette smoking from the model changed the estimate, indicating sensitivity to the adjustment set.
In this nationally representative sample of US adults, large eating episodes were more common among current cannabis users than among past or never users.

Among current users, reporting a large eating episode was associated with poorer self-rated health, which was the only one of 29 associations that remained significant after correction for multiple testing.
Further, poorer health was most evident among adults who had both current cannabis use and a large eating episode.
The excess risk of death was not significant after full adjustment.
Key findings are discussed below.
Large eating episodes became steadily more common from never users to past users to current users.

This gradient is consistent with laboratory evidence that cannabis increases both food intake and food reward (Farokhnia et al., 2020; Hume et al., 2026), and it also fits with clinical and survey evidence that links cannabis use to binge eating (Elran-Barak et al., 2025; Goodpaster, 2025; Wilkinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: This gradient is consistent with laboratory evidence that cannabis increases both food intake and food reward <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Farokhnia et al., 2020;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Hume et al., 2026)</ref>, and it also fits with clinical and survey evidence that links cannabis use to binge eating <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">(Elran-Barak et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">Goodpaster, 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">Wilkinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Past cannabis users fell between current and never users, a pattern that is consistent with an association tied to recent use.

Importantly, these results indicate that the link between cannabis use and large eating episodes extends beyond treatment-seeking and young adult samples to the general population of working-age adults.

As such, individuals who use cannabis and eat in this way will often be seen in primary care, nutrition, and substance use settings rather than in eating disorder clinics, and clinicians in those settings are well placed to ask about eating patterns in plain behavioral terms (e.g., whether a person ever eats an unusually large amount at one sitting).
Fair or poor self-rated health showed the clearest association with co-occurring cannabis use and large eating episodes.
Specifically, its prevalence among current cannabis users was 23.4% with a large eating episode and 17.8% without one.

Self-rated health summarizes physical, mental, and functional aspects of health; thus, poorer self-rated health may reflect more general health risks associated with co-occurring cannabis use and large eating episodes that single physical measures do not capture.

This association was not explained by the amount of energy intake and in fact became stronger after adjustment for average daily energy intake, suggesting that the pattern of eating carries information beyond total intake.
Lower diet quality among current users (Gelfand & Tangney, 2021) adds to this picture.
text.formatted: Lower diet quality among current users <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Gelfand & Tangney, 2021)</ref> adds to this picture.

text.text: For clinicians, this means that dietary counseling for adults who use cannabis should address how much an individual eats at one sitting and not only total calories or food choices, and a brief question about unusually large eating occasions could be added to routine intake and substance use screening.

Ecological momentary assessment (EMA) can record cannabis use, hunger, mood, and loss of control as each eating occasion occurs, and future studies should use EMA alongside dietary recalls to determine whether episodes follow cannabis use and whether they involve loss of control.

The four-group analysis showed that adults with both current cannabis use and a large eating episode had higher odds of fair or poor health than adults with neither exposure, adults with cannabis use alone, and adults with a large eating episode alone, whereas the other three groups had similar odds of fair or poor health.
Thus, only the combination of the two exposures stood apart.
This means that neither cannabis use nor a large eating episode alone identified poorer health in this sample.

The combination may mark a subgroup that is more vulnerable to the pathways described above (i.e., appetite and diet, loss of control and psychological distress, and food insecurity), and may also mark episodes that are driven by the appetite-inducing effects of cannabis.

While the formal test of whether the association differed across never, past, and current users did not remain significant after correction, the overall pattern is best interpreted as a description of who reports poorer health.

These findings do not show that cannabis use changes the effect of a large eating episode on health; rather, they identify a subset of patients who may warrant closer attention and targeted intervention.

Adults who report both cannabis use and large eating episodes could be prioritized for screening for distress, food insecurity, and disordered eating, and future trials could test whether brief interventions targeting cannabis use and eating behaviors improve health (e.g., helping adults plan regular meals and food access around cannabis use).
Notably, these associations depended on the calorie threshold chosen and were not significant at 1,000 or 2,000 kcal cut-offs.
A threshold of 1,000 kcal includes many ordinary large meals and likely mixes typical eating with unusual eating, thereby diluting any association.
Conversely, a threshold of 2,000 kcal includes very few eating occasions, meaning that this analysis had little power to detect an association at that level.
The 1,500 kcal threshold falls between these and was drawn from a clinical study (Keel et al., 2007).
text.formatted: The 1,500 kcal threshold falls between these and was drawn from a clinical study <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Keel et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: It appears to separate unusual eating occasions from ordinary ones while retaining enough power for detecting meaningful patterns.
Additionally, one large episode day was associated with fair or poor health, while two large episode days were not.
This pattern of findings should not be interpreted as evidence that recurrent episodes are harmless; rather, it suggests that a single large eating occasion is already informative.
For clinicians and patients, this means that an eating pattern does not need to be frequent or severe enough to meet criteria for an eating disorder to be associated with poorer health.
For researchers and surveillance systems, it means that adding a calorie threshold or a question about unusually large eating occasions to health surveys would allow the pattern to be monitored.
Associations with the other health outcomes were smaller.

Household food insecurity, obesity, abdominal obesity, and elevated glycated hemoglobin were each more common among cannabis users with a large eating episode before correction for multiple testing, and all four were in the direction of poorer health.
However, none remained significant after correction, and these findings should thus be treated as hypothesis-generating rather than confirmatory.
These findings are consistent with reports that binge eating is related to chronic physical conditions and to impaired glycemic control (Harris et al., 2021; Udo & Grilo, 2019).
text.formatted: These findings are consistent with reports that binge eating is related to chronic physical conditions and to impaired glycemic control <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Harris et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">Udo & Grilo, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: The food insecurity finding is also consistent with reports that food insecurity is linked to both binge eating and cannabis use (Abene et al., 2023; Chakraborty et al., 2025; Hazzard et al., 2020).
text.formatted: The food insecurity finding is also consistent with reports that food insecurity is linked to both binge eating and cannabis use <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Abene et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Chakraborty et al., 2025;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">Hazzard et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Interestingly, depressive symptoms were not clearly higher among adults with a large eating episode, which argues against a purely affective link between cooccurring cannabis use and binge eating and poor health outcomes, although it does not exclude other forms of distress that were not measured (e.g., shame and anxiety).

Most laboratory markers showed no clear association with a large eating episode, including fasting glucose, insulin resistance, triglycerides, HDL cholesterol, measured blood pressure, and C-reactive protein.
Earlier work found lower body mass index, less diabetes, and lower insulin resistance among cannabis users than among non-users (Jakob et al., 2024; Mousavi et al., 2023; Reis et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Earlier work found lower body mass index, less diabetes, and lower insulin resistance among cannabis users than among non-users <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Jakob et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Mousavi et al., 2023;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Reis et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Those studies compared users with nonusers, whereas we compared users with and without a large eating episode.
Large eating episodes among cannabis users were not accompanied by clear laboratory evidence of cardiometabolic disease; rather, the difference was seen in how adults rated their own health.
Two interpretations fit this pattern.
First, self-rated health may register early or functional effects before laboratory values change (e.g., fatigue or discomfort after large meals).
Second, the laboratory subsamples were smaller and had less power than the full sample.
Thus, clinicians should not rely on laboratory results alone to judge whether an eating pattern is affecting a patient, and should ask patients how they feel and how they rate their own health.
In exploratory mortality analyses, adults with both exposures had a twofold higher hazard of death than adults with neither after adjustment for age and sex.
However, this estimate was no longer significant after adjustment for social factors, cigarette smoking, alcohol, body mass index, energy intake, and chronic disease.
Conversely, the estimate was significant when only cigarette smoking was removed from the fully adjusted model.
Cigarette smoking is common among cannabis users (Xue et al., 2026) and strongly affects mortality (Thomson et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Cigarette smoking is common among cannabis users <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Xue et al., 2026)</ref> and strongly affects mortality <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Thomson et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, much of the mortality risk appears to reflect smoking and other shared risks.
Additionally, a meta-analysis found that larger cohort studies gave smaller mortality estimates for cannabis use (Alimoradi et al., 2025).
text.formatted: Additionally, a meta-analysis found that larger cohort studies gave smaller mortality estimates for cannabis use <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Alimoradi et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, excess mortality in cannabis use disorder was seen in adults who needed hospital care (Myran et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In contrast, excess mortality in cannabis use disorder was seen in adults who needed hospital care <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Myran et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: NHANES current users were not selected for hospital care and probably have less severe use; thus, a smaller excess risk would be expected in this sample.
The mortality findings are best interpreted as inconclusive and not as evidence that the combination is safe.
Given that the sample was young, deaths were few, and follow-up was short, the analysis had limited power to detect even a moderate risk.
These findings have important clinical implications.
Daily cannabis use is now common (Caulkins, 2024), and a growing share of adults is thus exposed to the appetite effects of cannabis (Hume et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Daily cannabis use is now common <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caulkins, 2024)</ref>, and a growing share of adults is thus exposed to the appetite effects of cannabis <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hume et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Clinicians who treat binge eating are already advised to screen for cannabis and alcohol use (Wilkinson et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Clinicians who treat binge eating are already advised to screen for cannabis and alcohol use <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Wilkinson et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Our results suggest that the reverse is also useful: providers in primary care, nutrition, and substance use settings can ask adults who use cannabis whether they ever eat unusually large amounts at one sitting and whether they worry about having enough food.
A positive answer could prompt a brief assessment of loss of control over eating, mood, and diet, as well as a referral to eating disorder or food assistance services.

Additionally, patients can be encouraged to plan regular meals and keep nutritious foods available when they use cannabis, given that the appetite effects of cannabis are predictable (Hume et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Additionally, patients can be encouraged to plan regular meals and keep nutritious foods available when they use cannabis, given that the appetite effects of cannabis are predictable <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Hume et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: For health systems, these findings support adding brief questions about eating patterns and food insecurity to cannabis screening and treatment programs, as well as to tobacco cessation programs, given that cannabis co-use is common in those programs (Xue et al., 2026).
text.formatted: For health systems, these findings support adding brief questions about eating patterns and food insecurity to cannabis screening and treatment programs, as well as to tobacco cessation programs, given that cannabis co-use is common in those programs <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Xue et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The reverse also applies, such that eating disorder and nutrition services can add routine questions about cannabis use.
Health systems can also build referral routes that connect cannabis, nutrition, food assistance, and mental health services, given that the pathways identified here cross all four.
For policy makers, the findings point to three actions.
First, public health messaging and information provided at the point of sale can describe the appetitive effects of cannabis and suggest planning for them.
Second, programs that improve food access can be extended to individuals who use cannabis, given that food insecurity is linked to both cannabis use and large eating episodes.

Third, national surveys can add dietary recalls and loss-of-control questions so that these patterns can be monitored as the cannabis market continues to change (Caulkins, 2024), and the role of binge eating psychopathology specifically can be clarified.
text.formatted: Third, national surveys can add dietary recalls and loss-of-control questions so that these patterns can be monitored as the cannabis market continues to change <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caulkins, 2024)</ref>, and the role of binge eating psychopathology specifically can be clarified.

text.text: Future research should directly test the proposed pathways between co-occurring cannabis use, binge eating, and poor health.

Specifically, longitudinal studies that measure loss of control, cannabis frequency, potency, and product type, as well as food insecurity and distress, at several time points can test 1) whether cannabis use precedes large eating episodes with or without loss of control and 2) whether each pathway explains the association with self-rated health, while EMA can be used to capture the timing of cannabis use relative to episodes.

Subsequently, trials should test whether interventions that reduce large eating episodes, reduce loss of control over eating, or improve food access improve self-rated health among adults who use cannabis.
The current study has several notable strengths.
First, it used a large nationally representative sample that spans 14 years.
Second, it examined a wide range of laboratory and questionnaire outcomes.
Third, we applied survey weights and a correction for multiple testing (Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995) and included several sensitivity analyses.
text.formatted: Third, we applied survey weights and a correction for multiple testing <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Benjamini & Hochberg, 1995)</ref> and included several sensitivity analyses.

text.text: Findings from the current study should be interpreted in light of several limitations.
First, the health outcomes were measured at the same time as large eating episodes, and as such the direction of association cannot be determined.
Second, dietary intake came from two 24-hour recalls.

Although the NHANES method was designed to reduce bias in reported energy intake (Moshfegh et al., 2008), self-reported energy intake is nevertheless underreported more often at higher body mass index (Ravelli & Schoeller, 2020), and underreporting of large episodes would weaken the associations we observed.
text.formatted: Although the NHANES method was designed to reduce bias in reported energy intake <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Moshfegh et al., 2008)</ref>, self-reported energy intake is nevertheless underreported more often at higher body mass index <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ravelli & Schoeller, 2020)</ref>, and underreporting of large episodes would weaken the associations we observed.

text.text: Two days also cannot capture usual behavior over longer timespans.
Third, NHANES does not measure the subjective sense of loss of control that is a diagnostic requirement of binge eating.
As such, many large eating occasions will not reflect binge eating pathology, and we cannot assume that our results generalize to binge-spectrum eating disorders.

Fourth, cannabis use was classified by recency, and we had no information on frequency, dose, product type, route of use, or cannabis use disorder, all of which influence the effect of cannabis on appetite (Goodpaster, 2025).
text.formatted: Fourth, cannabis use was classified by recency, and we had no information on frequency, dose, product type, route of use, or cannabis use disorder, all of which influence the effect of cannabis on appetite <ref type="bibr" target="#b15">(Goodpaster, 2025)</ref>.

text.text: Fifth, several estimates rested on small sample sizes, ranging from 268 to 2,414 across outcomes.

Two estimates (i.e., those for reported osteoporosis and glycated hemoglobin of at least 6.5%) were flagged as sparse because they had fewer than five outcome events or nonevents per fitted coefficient; these estimates are imprecise and should be interpreted with extreme caution.
Sixth, unmeasured factors (e.g., physical activity or use of other drugs) may have contributed to the associations and could represent unmeasured confounders.

Seventh, correction for multiple testing across 29 outcomes controls the false discovery rate, which lowers the chance of false positive findings but raises the chance of missing true modest associations.
Accordingly, the four outcomes that were significant only before correction may reflect real associations or chance and should be interpreted as hypothesis-generating.
Notably, the absence of significance for other outcomes should not be read as evidence of no association.
Finally, the participants were aged 20 to 59 years and data collection ended in 2018, and thus the results may not apply to adolescents or older adults.
Daily cannabis use has increased since 2018 (Caulkins, 2024), and the range of cannabis products and their legal status have also changed.
text.formatted: Daily cannabis use has increased since 2018 <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Caulkins, 2024)</ref>, and the range of cannabis products and their legal status have also changed.

text.text: If these changes strengthen the appetite effects of cannabis, the associations in current users could now be stronger than those we observed.
Thus, our estimates are best viewed as a baseline for the period before 2018 that can be updated as newer NHANES cycles become available.
In summary, large eating episodes were more common among current cannabis users and were associated with poorer self-rated health in this group.

Household food insecurity, obesity, abdominal obesity, and elevated glycated hemoglobin showed associations in the same direction that did not remain significant after correction for multiple testing.
Taken together, these findings indicate that specific eating patterns can identify a subgroup of adults who use cannabis and report poorer health.
Longitudinal studies that measure loss of control, cannabis frequency, and product type are critical next steps.
